::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Read [Your first composite model](diblock-copolymer.qmd) first. You should
be able to link endpoints, name a graph, and evaluate its form factor.
:::

The goal is to reuse a connected component without rebuilding its internal
links. We will make one diblock, then connect two instances through their
`polyA.end1` references. This two-arm component is named `star`.

```text
(polyB -- polyA) = (polyA -- polyB)
```

## Build and reuse the component

### 1. Create a world

All reusable graphs live in the same `World`. Later steps instantiate these
graphs without rebuilding their internal links.

```{python}
import pyseb

world = pyseb.World("NestedTutorial")
```

### 2. Build the reusable diblock

Start with `polyA`, then attach `polyB` end to end. Keep the returned graph in
`diblock`; a graph does not need a public structure name before it can be
reused.

```{python}
diblock = world.Add("GaussianPolymer", "polyA")
world.Link("GaussianPolymer", "polyB.end1", "polyA.end2")
```

### 3. Reuse the diblock to make a star

`world.Add(diblock, "diblock1")` creates the first instance. `Link` creates a
second instance and connects the `polyA.end1` reference inside each diblock.
The colon separates a structure instance from a nested subunit path.

```{python}
star = world.Add(diblock, "diblock1")
world.Link(diblock, "diblock2:polyA.end1", "diblock1:polyA.end1")
```

### 4. Parameterize, inspect, and evaluate

Repeated instances retain the internal names `polyA` and `polyB`. Consequently
all four polymers reuse four physical parameters.

```{python}
parameters = {
    "beta_polyA": 1.0,
    "beta_polyB": 0.75,
    "Rg_polyA": 5.0,
    "Rg_polyB": 8.0,
}
```

Name and inspect the reusable component. Hover over a curve to see its nested
instance path; repeated instances retain the internal subunit names.

```{python}
world.Add(star, "star")
_ = pyseb.visualize(world, "star", parameters, height=440)
```

```{python}
q = [0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3]
values = world.EvaluateFormFactor("star", parameters, q)

for q_value, value in zip(q, values):
    print(f"q={q_value:g}, F(q)={value:.8f}")
```

The decreasing values show the expected loss of coherence as q resolves the
nested structure's internal length scales.

You now have two instances of the same diblock. Their internal names share
parameters; their instance names identify which copy a reference belongs to.
